# Optimized model for modified Gram–Schmidt (QR) kernel

domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)         # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)         # column index for A and Q, and column index for R
    k: dim in [0, N)         # row index for R / current column being processed

data:
    # Column-major layout for A and Q (i contiguous) matches column-wise traversals.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i
    Q[i, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i

    # Row-major layout for R (j contiguous) matches row-wise writes R[k, j].
    R[k, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j

parameters:
    M: size_t                  # number of rows
    N: size_t                  # number of columns
    TI: size_t                 # tile size for i (rows), e.g., 128
    TJ: size_t                 # tile size for j (trailing columns), e.g., 32
    VI: size_t                 # SIMD width for i-vectorization
    UI: size_t                 # unroll factor for i

computation:
    # Outer loop over columns k (must remain sequential to respect A-dependences).
    for k in seq[0, N):

        # 1) Compute squared 2-norm of k-th column of A:
        #    nrm = sum_i A[i,k]^2
        nrm := 0
        norm_accumulate:
            for i in [0, M):
                nrm = nrm + A[i, k] * A[i, k]

        # 2) Normalize the k-th column and write Q[:,k], R[k,k]:
        #    rkk = sqrt(nrm)
        #    Q[i,k] = A[i,k] / rkk
        diag_and_Q:
            rkk := sqrt(nrm)
            R[k, k] = rkk

            # Precompute reciprocal to replace many divisions with multiplications.
            inv_rkk := 1 / rkk
            for i in [0, M):
                Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_rkk

        # 3) For each trailing column j > k, orthogonalize A[:,j] against Q[:,k]:
        for j in seq[k + 1, N):

            # 3a) r_kj = Q[:,k]^T * A[:,j]
            rkj := 0
            dot_accumulate:
                for i in [0, M):
                    rkj = rkj + Q[i, k] * A[i, j]

            # 3b) Store R[k,j]
            store_R:
                R[k, j] = rkj

            # 3c) Rank-1 update: A[:,j] -= Q[:,k] * R[k,j]
            update_A:
                for i in [0, M):
                    A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * rkj

dependencies:
    # k-iterations are serialized: later k depend on A updated by earlier k.
    for k1 in [0, N), k2 in [0, k1):
        # Any use of A in iteration k1 depends on all updates to A in iteration k2.
        for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
            update_A(k2, j, i) -> norm_accumulate(k1, i)
            update_A(k2, j, i) -> dot_accumulate(k1, j, i)

    # For fixed k, different trailing columns j > k are independent:
    # this enables safe parallelization across j (or across j-tiles).
    for k in [0, N), j1 in [k + 1, N), j2 in [k + 1, N):
        if j1 != j2:
            for i in [0, M):
                # No cross-dependence between work on columns j1 and j2.
                dot_accumulate(k, j1, i)  -> update_A(k, j1, i)
                dot_accumulate(k, j2, i)  -> update_A(k, j2, i)

optimization:
    # --- Data layout choices (already encoded in 'data') ---
    # A and Q are column-major so that column-wise loops over i touch contiguous memory.
    # R is row-major so that row-wise writes R[k, j] for fixed k use contiguous memory.

    # --- Loop tiling / blocking ---
    # Tile the row dimension to control working-set size and improve cache locality
    # for the accumulations and rank-1 updates on modern caches.
    block(i, I, TI)          # i = I * TI + i_local, TI tuned for L1/L2 (e.g., 64–256)

    # Tile the trailing-column dimension per k to create coarse-grain tasks that fit cache.
    # j = J * TJ + j_local, starting from j = k + 1 within each k-iteration.
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # --- Loop ordering / hoisting ---
    # Keep k as the outermost loop; within each k, iterate tiles J of trailing columns,
    # then tiles I of rows inside each column/tile.
    hoist(k)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling along rows ---
    # Within each i-tile, vectorize and unroll the innermost loops that:
    #   - accumulate nrm,
    #   - write Q[:,k],
    #   - accumulate r_kj,
    #   - and update A[:,j].
    vectorize(I, VI)         # map iterations over i_local onto SIMD lanes
    unroll(I, UI)            # unroll i_local to expose ILP and reduce loop overhead

    # --- Parallelism across trailing columns ---
    # For each fixed k, tiles of trailing columns J are independent and can be
    # processed in parallel on different threads / cores.
    parallelize(J)

    # --- Arithmetic optimizations ---
    # - Use 'inv_rkk = 1 / rkk' and compute Q[i,k] = A[i,k] * inv_rkk to replace
    #   M divisions per column with a single division and M multiplications.
    # - Keep reduction scalars (nrm, rkj) in registers within each loop nest to avoid
    #   redundant memory traffic.
    # - Optionally fuse adjacent loops over i within the same (k, j) or (k, J) region
    #   during code generation, as long as the data dependencies above are preserved.

    # --- Optional small temporaries (bounded extra memory) ---
    # - For each thread and (k, J)-tile, an on-stack buffer r_tile[0 .. TJ-1] can
    #   be used to hold r_kj values for the tile before writing them to R and
    #   updating A. This keeps R[k, j] hot in registers/cache and does not exceed
    #   O(TJ) extra storage per thread, well below 50% of the main data footprint.

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)       # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)       # column index
    k: dim in [0, N)       # column / R-row index

data:
    # A is modified in-place during Gram–Schmidt.
    # Use column-major layout so that all inner products over i see contiguous data.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i

    # Q stores the orthonormal basis vectors; same layout and access pattern as A.
    Q[i, j]: out DATA_TYPE   = (i, j) -> j * M + i

    # R is an upper-triangular N×N matrix. We keep it row-major because we update row k.
    R[k, j]: out DATA_TYPE   = (k, j) -> k * N + j

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters (chosen w.r.t. cache and SIMD width on the target machine)
    Ti: int > 0   # tile size along i (rows) for dot products and updates
    Tj: int > 0   # tile size along j (columns) in the orthogonalization phase
    VF: int > 0   # SIMD vector width (in elements) for i
    Ui: int > 0   # unroll factor for i within a tile

computation:
    # Modified Gram–Schmidt QR decomposition:
    #   A (M×N)  -> Q (M×N) with orthonormal columns, R (N×N) upper triangular,
    #   while A is overwritten with the evolving residual.
    for k in seq([0, N)):
        # 1) Compute the 2-norm of column k of A and store it on the diagonal of R.
        R[k, k] = sqrt( sum(i, A[i, k] * A[i, k]) )

        # 2) Normalize column k:
        #      Q[:, k] = A[:, k] / R[k, k]
        for i:
            Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]

        # 3) Orthogonalize remaining columns j > k against Q[:, k].
        for j in [k+1, N):
            # 3a) Compute R[k, j] = Q[:, k]^T * A[:, j]
            R[k, j] = sum(i, Q[i, k] * A[i, j])

            # 3b) Update A[:, j] ← A[:, j] − Q[:, k] * R[k, j]
            for i:
                A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # Layout choices:
    # - A and Q are column-major (affine mapping (i, j) -> j*M + i), making all column-wise
    #   operations over i (norms, dot products, and updates of A[:, *], Q[:, k]) contiguous.
    # - R is row-major ((k, j) -> k*N + j), so writes to a fixed row R[k, j] for j ≥ k are contiguous.

    # 1. Improve cache locality and enable SIMD over the reduction/update dimension i.
    block(i, Ii, Ti)          # strip-mine i into tiles of size Ti: i = Ii * Ti + (i % Ti)
    vectorize(i, VF)          # generate SIMD code over the innermost i-iterations
    unroll(i, Ui)             # unroll the scalar loop over i within each tile to reduce loop overhead

    # 2. Improve spatial locality and expose parallelism across columns j for each k.
    #    For fixed k, different j > k:
    #      - all read the same Q[:, k],
    #      - read and write disjoint columns A[:, j],
    #      - write disjoint R[k, j],
    #    so they are independent and can be executed in parallel.
    block(j, J, Tj)           # tile columns into blocks of size Tj to improve locality in A and R
    parallelize(J)            # execute column tiles J in parallel for each fixed k

    # 3. Respect algorithmic dependencies:
    #    - The outer loop over k must remain sequential (no parallelize(k), no reordering),
    #      because each step k uses the updated A and Q from all previous steps < k.
```

```text
domain:
    # M: number of rows, N: number of columns (M = M, N = N from the C++ code)
    i: dim in [0, M)              # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)              # column index (for A, Q, and R)
    k: dim in [0, N)              # column index / R row index

data:
    # A and Q are stored column-major: i is the contiguous dimension.
    # This matches the Noarr layout j_vec ^ i_vec and favors traversals over i for fixed j.
    A[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> j * M + i
    Q[i, j]: out   num_t = (i, j) -> j * M + i

    # R is stored row-major: j is the contiguous dimension.
    # This differs from the original Noarr layout (which was column-major in k),
    # but preserves mathematical semantics while making writes of R[k, j] for fixed k stream in memory.
    R[k, j]: out   num_t = (k, j) -> k * N + j

    # Temporary: reciprocal of diagonal of R to turn divides into multiplies.
    # Size O(N), negligible compared to A/Q/R, well below the +50% memory budget.
    invR[k]: temp  num_t = (k) -> k

parameters:
    M: size_t              # number of rows (PolyBench M)
    N: size_t              # number of columns (PolyBench N)

    # Tuning parameters (chosen per target machine, not fixed by semantics):
    TI: size_t             # tile size along i (e.g., 128) – sized for L1/L2 cache
    TJ: size_t             # tile size along j (e.g., 32)  – sized for LLC / NUMA
    VF: size_t             # SIMD vector width along i (e.g., 4 for AVX2 double, 8 for AVX-512)
    NUM_THREADS: size_t    # maximum number of worker threads used for parallel j-tiles

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization (init_array in the C++ code)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    init_A_Q:
        for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
            # A[i][j] = (((i*j) % M) / M) * 100 + 10;
            A[i, j] = (((i * j) mod M) / (num_t)M) * (num_t)100.0 + (num_t)10.0
            # Q[i][j] = 0.0;
            Q[i, j] = (num_t)0.0

    init_R:
        for k in [0, N), j in [0, N):
            # R[i][j] = 0.0;  (here indices are k,j)
            R[k, j] = (num_t)0.0

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Modified Gram-Schmidt (kernel_gramschmidt)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    gram_schmidt:
        # Outer loop over k must remain sequential: each step updates A and R
        # and subsequent k iterations depend on these updated values.
        for k in seq([0, N)):

            # 1) Compute squared 2-norm of k-th column of A and set diagonal R[k, k]
            #    nrm = sum_i A[i,k]^2; R[k,k] = sqrt(nrm);
            diag_nrm(k):
                R[k, k] = sqrt(sum(i in [0, M)) A[i, k] * A[i, k])

            # 2) Cache reciprocal 1 / R[k,k] to replace divides with multiplies.
            #    This mirrors the compiler optimization but is made explicit here.
            inv_diag(k):
                invR[k] = (num_t)1.0 / R[k, k]

            # 3) Normalize k-th column: Q[:,k] = A[:,k] / R[k,k]
            #    Q[i][k] = A[i][k] / R[k][k];
            normalize_column(k):
                for i in [0, M]:
                    Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * invR[k]

            # 4) Orthogonalize remaining columns j > k against q_k
            #    for (j = k+1; j < n; j++) { ... }
            for j in [k+1, N):

                # 4a) Compute R[k,j] = q_k^T * a_j
                #      r_kj = sum_i Q[i,k] * A[i,j];
                dot_R(k, j):
                    R[k, j] = sum(i in [0, M)) Q[i, k] * A[i, j]

                # 4b) Update A[:,j] := A[:,j] - q_k * R[k,j]
                #      A[i][j] = A[i][j] - Q[i][k] * R[k][j];
                update_A(k, j):
                    for i in [0, M):
                        A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Diagonal and normalization dependencies per k
    for k in [0, N):
        diag_nrm(k)      -> inv_diag(k)
        inv_diag(k)      -> normalize_column(k)

    # For each fixed (k, j) with j > k, the phases must order as in the source
    for k in [0, N), j in [k+1, N):
        normalize_column(k) -> dot_R(k, j)
        dot_R(k, j)         -> update_A(k, j)

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Data layout choices (expressed above in the data section)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # - A and Q use column-major storage: element (i, j) at address j*M + i.
    #   This makes traversals over i for fixed j contiguous, matching all
    #   inner loops in the algorithm (norms, normalizations, dot products,
    #   and updates). This improves cache utilization and SIMD efficiency.
    #
    # - R uses row-major storage: element (k, j) at address k*N + j.
    #   This optimizes the sequential writes R[k, j] for fixed k and
    #   increasing j inside the k-iteration (upper-triangular row), which
    #   were strided in the original Noarr layout.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Loop blocking (tiling) for cache and TLB locality
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # Block the row dimension i for all loops traversing columns:
    #  - diag_nrm: sum over i for fixed k  (column A[:,k])
    #  - normalize_column: for i over column A[:,k]
    #  - dot_R and update_A: for i over columns A[:,j], Q[:,k]
    # TI is tuned so that a tile of A/Q (and associated R/temps) fits nicely
    # into L1/L2 cache for a single thread.
    block(i, I, TI)

    # Block the column dimension j inside the j>k loop:
    #  - This groups columns A[:,j] and R[k,j] updates into smaller chunks
    #    so that working sets for one (k, J)-tile fit into shared caches.
    #  - The triangular constraint j > k is preserved by restricting j inside
    #    each tile to [max(k+1, J_start), J_end).
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization strategy
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # The outer k loop is explicitly sequential (seq), as later k depend on
    # the updates to A and R performed in earlier iterations.
    # For each fixed k:
    #
    # - Different columns j > k are independent:
    #   * Each j uses the same Q[:,k] and R[k,k], but reads/writes disjoint
    #     A[:,j] and R[k,j].
    #   * Therefore, j (or its tile index J) can be parallelized safely.
    #
    # We parallelize over column tiles J to get coarse-grain tasks suitable
    # for NUM_THREADS worker threads.
    parallelize(J)

    # Within a (k, J) tile, further parallelizing over I (tiles of rows)
    # can be beneficial for very tall matrices (M >> N). This introduces
    # parallel reductions over i in diag_nrm and dot_R. It is semantically
    # correct but requires an implementation that recognizes sum-reductions.
    parallelize(I)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # The innermost work across i inside each (k, j) or (k) tile is a
    # contiguous loop over A[i, *] and Q[i, *], well-suited for SIMD.
    # The following directive expresses that those loops should be vectorized:
    vectorize(i, VF)

    # Additionally, small unrolling factors along i (often equal to VF)
    # can reduce loop overhead and help the compiler schedule FMA pipelines.
    unroll(i, VF)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Arithmetic optimizations
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # 1) Replace division by R[k,k] with multiplication by its reciprocal invR[k].
    #    This is already encoded in the computation via invR[k].
    #
    # 2) Ensure FMA usage in inner products and updates:
    #    - dot_R(k,j): r_kj += Q[i,k] * A[i,j]
    #    - update_A(k,j): A[i,j] -= Q[i,k] * R[k,j]
    #
    #    With vectorize(i, VF), these become good candidates for fused
    #    multiply-add instructions, reducing both latency and rounding error.
```

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index for A and Q; also column index for R
    k: dim in [0, N)          # row index for R; current column in Gram–Schmidt

data:
    # Column‑major A and Q: fixed column j, varying i ⇒ unit‑stride accesses.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i + j * M
    Q[i, j]:   out DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i + j * M

    # Row‑major R: fixed row k, varying j ⇒ unit‑stride accesses.
    R[k, j]:   out DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j

parameters:
    M: size_t
    N: size_t

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization (matches init_array)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    init_A_Q:
        for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
            # A[i][j] = ((( (i*j) % M ) / M) * 100) + 10
            A[i, j] = (((DATA_TYPE)((i * j) mod M) / (DATA_TYPE)M) * (DATA_TYPE)100.0)
                      + (DATA_TYPE)10.0
            Q[i, j] = (DATA_TYPE)0.0

    init_R:
        for k in [0, N), j in [0, N):
            R[k, j] = (DATA_TYPE)0.0

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Modified Gram–Schmidt QR factorization
    # A is overwritten with the deflated columns, Q and R hold the factors.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    for k in seq[0, N):    # k must remain sequential (see dependencies)
        # --------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 1: squared 2‑norm of column k of A
        # nrm_k = sum_i A[i,k]^2
        # --------------------------------------------------------
        norm_k:
            nrm_k = sum(i in [0, M), A[i, k] * A[i, k])

        # --------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 2: normalize column k into Q[:,k], set diagonal R[k,k]
        # Q[i,k] = A[i,k] / R[k,k]
        # --------------------------------------------------------
        normalize_k:
            R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm_k)
            inv_rkk = (DATA_TYPE)1.0 / R[k, k]        # cheaper than a division per element
            for i in [0, M):
                Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_rkk

        # --------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 3: for each trailing column j>k
        #   R[k,j] = sum_i Q[i,k]*A[i,j]
        #   A[i,j] = A[i,j] - Q[i,k]*R[k,j]
        # --------------------------------------------------------
        for j in seq(k + 1, N):
            proj_kj:
                R[k, j] = sum(i in [0, M), Q[i, k] * A[i, j])
            update_A_kj:
                for i in [0, M):
                    A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Within a fixed k, the steps must execute in this order.
    for k in [0, N), j in [k + 1, N):
        norm_k(k)      -> normalize_k(k)
        normalize_k(k) -> proj_kj(k, j)
        proj_kj(k, j)  -> update_A_kj(k, j)

    # Across different k, column k2 uses A[:,k2] after all updates from k1<k2.
    for k1 in [0, N), k2 in [0, N):
        if k1 < k2:
            update_A_kj(k1, k2) -> norm_k(k2)

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Layout optimization
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Store A and Q in column‑major order so that all operations that
    # sweep columns (fixed j, varying i) are unit‑stride and vectorizable:
    #
    #   A[i,j], Q[i,j]  =>  offset = i + j * M
    #
    # This matches the dominant access pattern:
    #   - norm_k:      read A[:,k]
    #   - normalize_k: read A[:,k], write Q[:,k]
    #   - proj_kj:     read Q[:,k], A[:,j]
    #   - update_A_kj: read Q[:,k], R[k,j], update A[:,j]
    #
    # Keep R row‑major:
    #
    #   R[k,j] => offset = k * N + j
    #
    # which is optimal for writing the entire row R[k, k..N-1] in the
    # inner loops over j.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Tiling / blocking parameters (hardware‑tunable constants)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # TI  – tile size in i (rows), such that TI * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)
    #       fits well into L1 cache        (e.g., TI = 64).
    # TJ  – tile size in j (columns), such that TI * TJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)
    #       fits into L2 cache             (e.g., TJ = 32 or 64).
    # VI  – SIMD width in i (e.g., 8 for AVX2 doubles, 16 for AVX‑512 floats).
    # UIi – unrolling factor along i inside a tile (typ. 2–4).
    # UIj – unrolling factor along j inside a tile (typ. 2–4).

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Block i and j inside the k‑loop
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Work on cache‑resident tiles of the trailing submatrix A[:, k+1:].
    block(i, I, TI)      # I indexes row tiles of height TI
    block(j, J, TJ)      # J indexes column tiles of width TJ

    # Conceptual effect on Step 3 (for fixed k):
    #
    #   Original:
    #       for j in [k+1, N):
    #           r = sum_i Q[i,k]*A[i,j]
    #           for i: A[i,j] -= Q[i,k]*r
    #
    #   Tiled variant:
    #       # zero row R[k, j] for j>k once per k
    #       for j in [k+1, N):
    #           R[k,j] = 0.0
    #
    #       # accumulate partial sums over i tiles
    #       for I in [0, M) step TI:
    #         for J in [k+1, N) step TJ:
    #           for j in J:
    #             for i in I:
    #               R[k,j] += Q[i,k] * A[i,j]
    #
    #       # apply the rank‑1 update with the final R[k,j]
    #       for I in [0, M) step TI:
    #         for J in [k+1, N) step TJ:
    #           for j in J:
    #             for i in I:
    #               A[i,j] -= Q[i,k] * R[k,j]
    #
    # This preserves semantics (just a re‑association of the sum over i)
    # while improving temporal locality on A and R. The additional passes
    # use the same data and do not exceed the original asymptotic work.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Loop hoisting / ordering
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Keep k outermost to respect the algorithmic dependency between columns.
    hoist(k)

    # Within each k, outer tiles first, then elements inside tiles.
    hoist(J)   # process one column tile at a time
    hoist(I)   # within each J, process row tiles

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Parallelization
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # For a fixed k:
    #   - Different columns j>k are independent (given Q[:,k]), so tiles J
    #     can be processed in parallel.
    #   - Reductions over i (in norm_k and proj_kj) can be parallelized with
    #     a reduction on the accumulation variable.
    #
    # Parallelize tiles of columns in Step 3:
    parallelize(J)       # across column tiles J for each k

    # Parallelize reductions over i:
    #   - norm_k:    nrm_k = sum_i A[i,k]^2
    #   - proj_kj:   R[k,j] += sum_i Q[i,k]*A[i,j] (with reduction into R[k,j])
    parallelize(i)       # use a reduction on nrm_k and on partial R[k,j]

    # (k itself remains sequential, per dependencies.)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Vectorization and unrolling
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # With column‑major A and Q, i is unit‑stride and ideal for SIMD.
    vectorize(i, VI)
    unroll(i, UIi)

    # For short inner loops over j inside a tile, unroll to expose ILP:
    unroll(j, UIj)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Strength reduction and invariant hoisting
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # - Compute inv_rkk = 1.0 / R[k,k] once per k and use a multiply
    #   Q[i,k] = A[i,k] * inv_rkk instead of a division per i.
    # - Hoist Q[i,k] loads out of the inner j‑loops where possible:
    #     for fixed (k, i) and a tile J of columns,
    #     keep Q[i,k] in a register and reuse it across all j in J,
    #   minimizing memory traffic for Q.
```

domain:
    # Matrix dimensions
    i: dim in [0, M)        # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)        # column index of A,Q and R
    k: dim in [0, N)        # column index / iteration index in Gram–Schmidt

data:
    # NOTE: We choose layouts tuned to the access patterns of the kernel, not to the original Noarr tuning.
    #       The original code accesses entire *columns* of A and Q (A[:,k], A[:,j], Q[:,k]) very frequently.
    #       Making columns contiguous (column-major) maximizes spatial locality and vectorization.
    #
    # A and Q: M x N, column-major (columns contiguous)
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i
        # A is modified in-place by Gram–Schmidt.
    Q[i, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i
        # Q is completely overwritten by the kernel, so its initial values are irrelevant.

    # R: N x N, row-major (rows contiguous)
    R[k, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j
        # We iterate over j for a fixed k, so row-major is cache-friendly.

parameters:
    M: std::size_t        # number of rows
    N: std::size_t        # number of columns

computation:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization (matches init_array, but drops dead initialization of Q)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------

    init_A:
        # for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
        for i, j:
            A[i, j] = (((DATA_TYPE)((i * j) mod M) / (DATA_TYPE)M) * (DATA_TYPE)100.0)
                      + (DATA_TYPE)10.0

    init_Q:
        # The original code zeroes Q here, but kernel_gramschmidt overwrites
        # every Q[i,j]. Keeping it as an explicit step is optional; we mark it
        # as dead-code removable in optimization.
        for i, j:
            Q[i, j] = (DATA_TYPE)0.0

    init_R:
        # for k in [0, N), j in [0, N):  R[k][j] = 0
        for k, j:
            R[k, j] = (DATA_TYPE)0.0

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Modified Gram–Schmidt QR decomposition
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    #
    # For each k:
    #   1. Compute the norm of column k of A and set R[k,k].
    #   2. Normalize A[:,k] into Q[:,k].
    #   3. For each j > k, compute R[k,j] and update column j of A.
    #
    # Data dependencies:
    #   - k loop is sequential: iteration k+1 consumes the updated A from
    #     iteration k.
    #   - For fixed k, operations over different (i,j) pairs are independent
    #     except for the scalar reductions (nrm and r_kj).

    gram_schmidt:
        for k in seq([0, N)):      # sequential in k (loop-carried deps via A and R)

            # --- 1. Column norm of A[:,k] and diagonal R[k,k] ----------------
            # nrm(k) = sum_i A[i,k] * A[i,k]
            nrm_k(k) = 0.0
            for i:
                nrm_k(k) += A[i, k] * A[i, k]

            # R[k,k] = sqrt(nrm_k)
            R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm_k(k))

            # Micro-opt: precompute reciprocal of R[k,k] to avoid per-element divides
            inv_r_kk(k) = 1.0 / R[k, k]

            # --- 2. Normalize column k: Q[:,k] = A[:,k] / R[k,k] -------------
            q_scale:
                for i:
                    # original: Q[i,k] = A[i,k] / R[k,k]
                    Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_r_kk(k)

            # --- 3. For each j > k, compute R[k,j] and update A[:,j] ---------
            update_future_columns:
                for j:
                    if j > k:
                        # Dot product: R[k,j] = sum_i Q[i,k] * A[i,j]
                        r_kj(k, j) = 0.0
                        for i:
                            r_kj(k, j) += Q[i, k] * A[i, j]
                        R[k, j] = r_kj(k, j)

                        # Rank-1 update of column j: A[:,j] -= Q[:,k] * R[k,j]
                        for i:
                            A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # ============================================================
    # Data-layout optimization
    # ============================================================

    # A and Q are declared column-major in `data`:
    #     (i, j) -> j * M + i
    # This makes all column slices A[:,j], Q[:,j] contiguous in memory,
    # which is exactly what the Gram–Schmidt algorithm uses.
    #
    # R is row-major:
    #     (k, j) -> k * N + j
    # which matches its use as R[k, j] with j varying fastest.

    # ============================================================
    # Arithmetic and scalar optimizations
    # ============================================================

    # Replace per-element division in Q update with a single reciprocal:
    #   inv_r_kk(k) = 1.0 / R[k,k]
    #   Q[i,k] = A[i,k] * inv_r_kk(k)
    #
    # This trades M divisions per column for 1 division + M multiplications,
    # which is faster on typical hardware while remaining numerically close
    # to the original behavior.
    #
    # (Already reflected in the `computation` section.)

    # Optionally mark Q initialization as dead:
    #   - Q is fully overwritten by gram_schmidt.
    #   - Remove `init_Q` to avoid a full M*N zero-fill.
    #
    # This reduces memory traffic and startup cost without changing
    # the behavior of the kernel.

    # ============================================================
    # Loop blocking and vectorization
    # ============================================================

    # Tunable tile sizes (hardware dependent):
    #   TI: tile size along rows (i), e.g., 64 or 128
    #   TJ: tile size along columns (j), e.g., 32 or 64
    #   VEC_I: SIMD width along i, e.g., 8 for AVX2 double / 16 for AVX2 float
    #   UNROLL_I: small integer multiple of VEC_I for unrolling

    # --- Row blocking and vectorization for all i-loops ----------------------
    #
    # We tile and vectorize the i-dimension in all three places it appears:
    #   - norm computation over A[:,k]
    #   - scaling Q[:,k]
    #   - dot products and column updates for j > k
    #
    # This improves cache reuse along columns and exposes SIMD-friendly
    # contiguous access (since A and Q are column-major).

    block(i, I, TI)
        # Conceptually: i = I * TI + i_inner, with i_inner in [0, TI)
        # Used in:
        #   - nrm_k(k) accumulation over i
        #   - Q[i,k] scaling loop
        #   - r_kj(k,j) accumulation over i
        #   - A[i,j] update loop

    hoist(I)
        # Move the tile-loop I outside of the inner i loops, but remain
        # inside the current k and j loops, so that:
        #   - For fixed (k,j), we iterate over row tiles I, then over
        #     the inner i within each tile.
        #   - Reductions over i are performed as:
        #       for I: partial_sum_I = sum(i in tile I) ...
        #     then combined across tiles (this can be implemented as
        #     accumulating into the same scalar across tiles).

    vectorize(i, VEC_I)
        # Vectorize the innermost i-loop (within a tile) for:
        #   - accumulation in nrm_k(k)
        #   - accumulation in r_kj(k,j)
        #   - element-wise Q and A updates

    unroll(i, UNROLL_I)
        # Unroll the innermost i-loop to reduce loop overhead and
        # expose more ILP. UNROLL_I should be a multiple of VEC_I.

    # ============================================================
    # Column blocking and parallelism in j for fixed k
    # ============================================================

    # Inside gram_schmidt, for a fixed k, each column j>k is updated
    # independently:
    #   - r_kj(k,j) depends only on Q[:,k] and A[:,j].
    #   - The A[:,j] update uses only these and R[k,j].
    #
    # There are no dependencies between different j in the same k
    # iteration, so we can tile and parallelize j.

    block(j, J, TJ)
        # Conceptually: j = J * TJ + j_inner
        # Apply only to the loops in `update_future_columns` (step 3).

    hoist(J)
        # For each k, iterate over column tiles J outermost, then within
        # each tile iterate over the inner j indices and the row tiles I.
        # This improves reuse of Q[:,k] across many columns A[:,j] that
        # are being processed in the same tile.

    parallelize(J)
        # Run different column tiles (J) in parallel for a fixed k.
        # Each thread (or core) owns a disjoint set of columns j, and
        # thus disjoint slices:
        #   - R[k, j]
        #   - A[:, j]
        # All threads read the shared Q[:,k], which is read-only.
        #
        # This yields thread-level parallelism without changing the
        # order of floating-point operations within each (k,j) pair.

    # Optionally:
    parallelize(i) in init_A
    parallelize(k) in init_R
        # Both initializations are element-wise and have no dependencies;
        # they can be fully parallelized over their respective dimensions.

    # ============================================================
    # Summary of resulting execution structure
    # ============================================================
    #
    # After applying the above optimizations, a typical schedule is:
    #
    #   for k in seq([0, N)):
    #       # 1) Norm and normalization of column k (i-tiled & vectorized)
    #       for I in [0, ceil(M/TI)):
    #           for i in [I*TI, min((I+1)*TI, M)):
    #               nrm_k(k) += A[i,k] * A[i,k]
    #       R[k,k] = sqrt(nrm_k(k))
    #       inv_r_kk(k) = 1.0 / R[k,k]
    #       for I:
    #           for i in [I*TI, ...):      # vectorized & unrolled
    #               Q[i,k] = A[i,k] * inv_r_kk(k)
    #
    #       # 2) Parallel update of future columns
    #       parallel for J in [0, ceil(N/TJ)):
    #           for j in [J*TJ, min((J+1)*TJ, N)):
    #               if j > k:
    #                   # r_kj reduction over i (tiled & vectorized)
    #                   r_kj(k,j) = 0
    #                   for I:
    #                       for i in [I*TI, ...):   # vectorized
    #                           r_kj(k,j) += Q[i,k] * A[i,j]
    #                   R[k,j] = r_kj(k,j)
    #
    #                   # A[:,j] update over i (tiled & vectorized)
    #                   for I:
    #                       for i in [I*TI, ...):   # vectorized
    #                           A[i,j] -= Q[i,k] * R[k,j]
    #
    # This schedule preserves the original algorithmic structure and
    # dependencies while:
    #   - Aligning memory layout with access patterns (column-major A,Q;
    #     row-major R),
    #   - Reducing expensive divisions via scalar reciprocals,
    #   - Exploiting SIMD via row-wise vectorization,
    #   - Exploiting multi-core parallelism via column tiling and
    #     parallelization of independent j-tiles for each k.
